transcript: . - Henrico County public schools officials are telling the citizen that all three of the proposed hybrid learning plans for public school students who choose to return to in-person learning this fall will include five days of instruction. Now that's different than what Henrico schools chief of staff that TIGEN outlined on Thursday during a virtual school board work session. On that day, she described each of the three plans as involving four days of learning for all students while Mondays would be reserved for a half day work period for teachers and a half day for additional support for those students who needed it. We sought clarification yesterday and Henrico schools spokesman Andy Jenks relayed to us clarification from TIGEN indicating that all students in each of the three plans actually would be learning on Mondays too, whether in school or virtually. As TIGEN described the three plans Thursday, one would involve a group of students who attended school in person Tuesdays and Thursdays and then worked virtually from home on Wednesdays and Fridays while a second group of students did the opposite. The second plan would involve the first group attending school in the mornings on Tuesday through Friday then learning virtually each afternoon while the other group did the opposite. And the third plan would have one group attending school in person Tuesday through Friday for one entire week and then learning virtually the following week while the other group did the opposite. Now it's unclear whether TIGEN on Thursday simply failed to include additional information about virtual learning plans for all students on Mondays or if the school system has updated those plans in the days since that meeting. In addition to the three hybrid plans, families will have the option to keep their students at home learning virtually five days a week. Those who select that option will be assigned to specific teachers who will be teaching virtual classes only, TIGEN said. The Henrico School Board and Board of Supervisors tonight will hold a joint work session at 5 p.m. in the Glen Allen High School Commons. The meeting is open to the public though no comments will be accepted. It also will be live streamed through WebEx. You can visit HenricoCitizen.com and click education to find this article for a link. Henrico County Police Chief Home Cardinal Jr. yesterday announced his plans to retire effective September 1st, the decision will end his nearly 32 year career with the division during which he served past four as its leader. Cardinal revealed his plans in an email to division staff members yesterday saying he would take advantage of the county's voluntary retirement incentive program, a cost cutting measure available during the pandemic that offers enhanced benefits to eligible employees who choose to retire. County manager John Vitocas praised Cardinal for his quote more than three decades of outstanding service and his calm, steady leadership as chief end quote. Cardinal joined the division as a patrol officer and SWAT team medic in 1988 and rose through the ranks to investigator and later sergeant, command sergeant, lieutenant, captain and major. He was named chief of police in 2016. County officials will conduct a national search for the next police chief and expect to make an appointment by September 1st. The number of first time unemployment filings in Henrico fell for the 10th straight week, according to data released last week by the Virginia Employment Commission, a total of 792 county residents filed initial unemployment claims during the week of June 7th through 13th. That was down about 18% from the previous week. Henrico's total was the eight highest among state localities. In the 13 weeks of filing data since the pandemic began in March, a total of more than 31,000 county residents have filed initial claims. That number is seventh highest in the state, just behind Richmond and Chesterfield. But fewer than half of those first time filers continued to file claims during the most recent week, according to the VDC, that suggests that at least some of them may have returned to work. The one Henrico woman is glad she had a headache. Olga Ritchie went to the Tony's market at 37-14 Mechanicville Turnpike in Henrico to pick up some headache powder as a result. And while she was there, she decided to buy a mega money ticket from the Virginia Lottery. She got home and scratched the ticket to discover that she had just won the game's top prize, $500,000. Ritchie, who has worked at the same place for more than 40 years, said she plans to save her winnings and use them toward retirement. She's also planning to upgrade her house. Good news for coffee lovers in Eastern Henrico, Starbucks will be opening a freestanding location at the shops at White Oak Village in Eastern Henrico, taking the place of a former Steak and Shake at the site, according to Varina District Supervisor Tyrone Nelson. Steak and Shake closed its location at White Oak in the fall of 2018 for remodeling, but never reopened before closing permanently later that year. The one acre's site has been empty since. It's owned by Burger Busters, a regional Taco Bell franchisee in Virginia Beach that also operates stakes of Virginia, which owns and operates at the Steak and Shake locations in the state. Starbucks currently operates two smaller in-store locations at White Oak Village inside Target and Publix, according to its website. Henrico Congressman Donald McEachin and a few other members of the Congressional Black Caucus yesterday convened a virtual town hall meeting to discuss how upcoming policy can address the concerns of black Americans. McEachin discussed the Environmental Justice for All Act, which he introduced in February. The bill would help marginalized communities keep their air, water and homes safe from industrial development. Steak and McEachin, quote, "When you look at why black and brown people are so adversely affected by COVID-19, you understand that it attacks the respiratory system. Black, brown and poor folks live near places with bad water, bad air, they're subject to stay at home orders, which are well intended, but they have to stay at home in public housing, which oftentimes isn't properly ventilated. It's subject to mold and is subject to making their respiratory systems even worse," end quote. You can read details about last night's meeting on HenricoCitizen.com. And Henrico Citizen managing editor Patty Kraseski has won a second place award in the National Federation of Press Women Competition. Her feature story, "A Beacon of Light Laughter," was one of two entries that advanced to national competition after winning first place awards in the Virginia Professional Communicators 2020 Communications contest. The story paid tribute to a Mekong bartender who drowned during a triathlon last year. Today's Henrico Newsmen, it has been brought to you by the Lakeside Farmers Market at 6110 Lakeside Avenue. It's open every Wednesday from 9 to 2 in Saturday from 9 to noon, so make plans to check it out tomorrow. Visit facebook.com/lakesidemarketRVA for details and a complete list of vendors. One hybrid plan involves alternating in-person attendance on Tuesdays and Thursdays with virtual learning on Wednesdays and Fridays.

The third hybrid plan uses a weekly rotation where one group attends in person for a full week and learns virtually the next, with the other group doing the reverse.
Families may opt for fully virtual learning five days a week, taught by dedicated virtual-only teachers.
